title: Set
content: A collection of well-defined objects or elements. Think of it like a basket of fruits from Chisokone market.
zambian_analogy: A collection of well-defined objects or elements. Think of it like a basket of fruits from Chisokone market.

subject: mathematics
title: Empty Set
content: A set with no elements. Denoted by {} or ∅. Like a wallet when it's month-end but the salary hasn't dropped!
zambian_analogy: A set with no elements. Denoted by {} or ∅. Like a wallet when it's month-end but the salary hasn't dropped!

subject: mathematics
title: Intersection
content: The set of elements that are common to two or more sets. Symbolized by ∩. Like items sold at both a kantemba and a big shop.
zambian_analogy: The set of elements that are common to two or more sets. Symbolized by ∩. Like items sold at both a kantemba and a big shop.

subject: mathematics
title: Union
content: The set containing all elements of all sets being considered. Symbolized by ∪. Bringing all your small baskets into one big heap.
zambian_analogy: The set containing all elements of all sets being considered. Symbolized by ∪. Bringing all your small baskets into one big heap.

title: Integer
content: A whole number that can be positive, negative, or zero. Negative integers are like having a debt (kaloba) at the local shop.

title: Equation

title: Variable

subject: mathematics
title: Introduction: Understanding Sets through Our Market
content:
Iyee, my champion! Today we're going to learn about Sets using something every Zambian understands - our market basket! Imagine you're at Kitwe Market or Soweto Market, and you need to organize different items for your family.

### What is a Set?

A **Set** is simply a collection of distinct objects, just like a market basket contains different items. In mathematics, we call these items **elements**.

**Example:**
- Set A = {guavas, mangoes, rape, tomatoes}
- Each item is an element of the set
zambian_analogy: Using Kitwe / Soweto market baskets to understand sets and intersections.

subject: mathematics
title: Types of Sets with Market Examples
content:
### 1. Empty Set (Null Set) - ∅ or {}
This is like an empty basket waiting to be filled!

**Market Example:** You arrive at the market with an empty basket. 
- Set B = {} (empty basket)
- You haven't bought anything yet!

### 2. Finite Sets
Sets with a countable number of elements.

**Market Example:** Your basket after shopping:
- Set C = {2 guavas, 3 mangoes, 1 bunch rape, 4 tomatoes}
- You can count exactly what you have

### 3. Infinite Sets
Sets that go on forever (less common in market situations, but important in math!)
zambian_analogy: Using Kitwe / Soweto market baskets to understand sets and intersections.

title: Set Operations: Market Mathematics

subject: mathematics
title: Venn Diagrams: Market Visuals
content:
Think of Venn diagrams as circles representing different baskets:

```
    Basket A          Basket B
   +---------+      +---------+
   | Guavas  |      | Onions  |
   | Mangoes |------| Tomatoes|  <-- Overlap = Intersection
   | Rape    |      | Carrots |
   +---------+      +---------+
```
zambian_analogy: Using Kitwe / Soweto market baskets to understand sets and intersections.

subject: mathematics
title: Practice Problems: Market Challenges
content:
### Problem 1:
At Chisokone Market, Mary bought {guavas, mangoes, tomatoes} while James bought {mangoes, onions, rape}. Find:
- Mary ∪ James (total items bought)
- Mary ∩ James (items both bought)

### Problem 2:
A farmer has {cows, goats, chickens, ducks}. He sells the cows and goats. What's left? (Use set difference)

### Problem 3:
If the universal set is all Grade 9 subjects {Math, English, Science, History, Geography, Bemba} and Set F = {Math, Science, Geography}, what is F'?
zambian_analogy: Using Kitwe / Soweto market baskets to understand sets and intersections.

title: Real-Life Applications
content:
1. **Inventory Management:** Shopkeepers use sets to track what's in stock
2. **Recipe Planning:** Combining ingredients from different sources
3. **Budget Planning:** Grouping expenses into categories
4. **Class Organization:** Grouping students by different subjects

title: Zambian Proverb Connection
content:
*"Amano mambulwa"* (Wisdom is picked up piece by piece) - Just like collecting items in your market basket, you collect mathematical concepts one by one!

subject: mathematics
title: INTRODUCTION
content: Mathematics, as a fundamental STEM subject, which plays an important role in shaping learners' understanding of the natural world. As learners transition from upper primary to secondary education, it is necessary to provide them with an all-inclusive and engaging introduction to Mathematics. Therefore, the Mathematics II Teaching Module for Form 2 is a comprehensive educational resource designed to support the teaching and learning of Mathematics for learners in their first year of secondary education. It covers fundamental concepts and principles of Mathematics, aligning with the 2024 Mathematics syllabus. The module includes topic and subtopic overviews, suggested teaching and learning materials, environment set-up, learning activities, and assessment guides. Additionally, it incorporates teaching methods and strategies like inquiry-based learning, problem-solving activities, group discussions, hands-on activities, multimedia resources, and interactive simulations. The aim is to provide a solid foundation in Mathematics, foster critical thinking and problem-solving skills, and inspire further studies in Mathematics.

title: SAFETY IN THE LEARNING ENVIRONMENT
content: Safety in the learning environment is a requirement in learning Mathematics, as learners are exposed to potential hazards during hands-on activities. Collaboration between teachers, and learners, is important to create a responsible learning environment that promotes scientific inquiry. Guidelines for maintaining a safe learning environment include, risk identification, personal protective equipment, emergency response plans, storage, disposal, and learner responsibilities. Prioritising safety minimises risks, prevents accidents, and ensures a positive learning experience.

title: Introduction
content: In Form 2, learners are expected to deal with basic processes of Algebra, such as factorising by grouping terms, quadratic expression, and difference of two squares. They are also expected to add, subtract, multiply and divide algebraic fractions, and simplify algebraic fractions using the Lowest Common Multiples (LCM) and factorisation. These basic processes help learners think logically, solve problems, and apply Mathematics to real-life situations. Algebra also provides a foundation for more advanced topics in Mathematics.

title: Introduction
content: Algebra is the language we use to describe patterns and relationships in everyday life. From the number of tiles in a growing design, the cost of buying several items, or the distance travelled over time, patterns help us to predict what comes next. In this unit, it is important to let learners explore number and visual patterns, identify relationships between quantities, and express these relationships using algebraic expressions and simple formulae. By recognising how quantities change together, learners develop the foundation for understanding variables, equations, and functions. subject: mathematics
title: Introduction
content: Algebraic fractions are fractions in which the numerator, the denominator, or both contain algebraic expressions instead of just numbers. Like numerical fractions, algebraic fractions can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided, but they require additional skills such as factorisation, identifying restrictions, and finding common denominators. Understanding operations on algebraic fractions help learners to simplify complex expressions, solve algebraic equations, model real-life situations (such as, rates, ratios, speed, density, financial formulas), and build a foundation for calculus and advanced algebra.

subject: mathematics
title: Introduction
content: The remainder and factor theorems are important concepts in Algebra because they help learners to understand the relationship between polynomial division and factorisation. These theorems provide a quicker and more meaningful way of determining the remainder when a polynomial is divided by a linear expression, and of checking whether a given expression is a factor of a polynomial. Through this topic, learners develop the ability to simplify polynomial work, factorise cubic expressions, and solve cubic as well as identical cubic equations in an efficient and logical manner.

source.document: Mathematics 2 Teaching Module for Term 2 2026 final Submission.json

subject: mathematics
title: Introduction
content: The study of the remainder and factor theorems also strengthens learners' reasoning, analytical thinking, and problem-solving skills. It enables them to see patterns in algebraic expressions and apply algebraic ideas to both classroom and real-life situations. In this topic, learners will explore the remainder and factor theorems, use them to find quotient and remainder, factorise cubic expressions, solve cubic equations, and use ICT tools to enhance understanding.

source.document: Mathematics 2 Teaching Module for Term 2 2026 final Submission.json

subject: mathematics
title: Introduction
content: Instead of performing lengthy polynomial division every time, mathematicians use two powerful tools, namely the Remainder Theorem and the Factor Theorem. These theorems provide efficient shortcuts that connect algebraic division with simple substitution, thereby transforming a complex procedure into a quick calculation. This section explores how and why these theorems work, helping learners move from procedural understanding to conceptual mastery.

subject: mathematics
title: Introduction
content: Overview: Variation in Mathematics describes the relationship between two quantities and how a change in one quantity affects the other. It helps learners understand how variables are connected and how mathematical models can represent real-life situations. In this topic, learners explore different types of relationships between variables such direct, inverse, joint, and partial variations. They learn how to express these relationships using mathematical equations, tables and graphs. For example, when two quantities increase or decrease together at a constant rate, they are said to vary directly. When one quantity increases while the other decreases, they vary inversely. Understanding variation helps learners apply Mathematics to real-life situations such as, speed and time relationships, cost and quantity relationships, pressure and volume in science, and other proportional relationships.

subject: mathematics
title: Terms /Words/Vocabulary:
content: Variation: A relationship between two or more variables where a change in one affects the other. Variable: A symbol (usually a letter) that represents a quantity that can change. Constant of Variation: A fixed number that relates the variables in a variation equation. Direct Variation: When two quantities increase or decrease together in the same proportion. Inverse Variation: When one quantity increases while the other decreases proportionally. Joint Variation: When one variable varies directly with two or more variables. Partial Variation: A relationship between variables where one variable changes partly in direct proportion to another variable and partly as a constant (fixed amount). Proportional Relationships: A relationship where two quantities maintain a constant ratio. Equation of Variation: A mathematical expression that represents the relationship between variables. Graph of Variation: A visual representation of the relationship between variables on a coordinate plane.

title: Introduction
content: Types of variation help learners understand how quantities change in relation to each other. This knowledge is important for solving practical problems in everyday life and for developing strong mathematical skills. The main types of variation are direct, inverse, joint, and partial variations. These are widely used in real-life situations such as, wages and hours worked, speed and travel time, number of workers and time taken to complete a job, force in physics, intensity of light, and many others.

subject: mathematics
title: Curriculum Objective: Introduction
content: In everyday life, many quantities are related and change together. Understanding how these quantities are connected helps learners make sense of the world around them. In mathematics, these relationships are often studied through proportions and variations, where one quantity changes depending on another. For example, as children grow older, their height generally increases, the temperature of water may change with depth, and the length of a shadow changes depending on the position of the sun during the day. Through exploring related proportions in the environment, learners develop important competences such as critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, observation, and data interpretation. This approach not only strengthens their mathematical understanding but also helps them appreciate how mathematics is applied in daily life.

Understanding types of variation helps learners to recognise how quantities relate in real-life situations. Through investigation, experimentation, and real-world simulations learners can understand how variables relate, and that helps us to predict outcomes, model-real-world situations, and solve practical problems in fields such as science, economics, and engineering.

title: Introduction
content: Through practical activities, learners discover that variation describes how quantities change in relation to each other. By using graphs, these relationships become easier to understand, interpret, and apply in everyday life such as shopping, travel, and construction. Graphical representation therefore becomes an important mathematical tool for analysing patterns and making predictions.

title: Item 3: Scenario
content: Chaona is a farmer in Kabwe rural and supplies maize to a milling company that produces mealie meal for sale in nearby markets including Lusaka and Ndola. She records production, transportation and milling costs using mathematical models to help her plan operations efficiently.

source.document: Mathematics 2 Teaching Module for Term 2 2026 final Submission.json

subject: mathematics
title: Item 3: Scenario
content: Chaona has three major farms A, B, and C that supply maize to the milling plant. The maize is processed into three products namely Breakfast meal, Roller meal, and Bran. The cost of transporting maize from the farms to the milling plant depends on fuel usage and distance. The transport manager models the cost per tonne using the expression \frac{2x}{x^2-9} + \frac{3}{x+3} - \frac{1}{x-3}, where x represents the fuel adjustment factor. She notices that there are instances when the transport manager is having difficulties in calculate the transportation costs. She needs help in finding such instances.

subject: mathematics
title: State Pythagoras' theorem
content: The Egyptians, Babylonians and Chinese from long ago knew of a special connection between the lengths of the sides of triangles and they used this relationship. However, the first person to define this relationship was Pythagoras, a Greek mathematician and philosopher (582 BC–500 BC). He established a school of philosophy in Italy where he and his followers expressed views that were considered strange at the time (such as that the earth rotates around its own axis and that the planets revolve around the sun). As a result of these theories, Pythagoras was forced to flee to Egypt.

subject: mathematics
title: Pythagoras' theorem states:
content: In any right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse is equal to the sum of the squares on the adjacent sides.

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • In a right-angled triangle, the area of the shape on the longest side is equal to the sum of the areas of similar shapes on the other two sides (the sides adjacent to the right angle).

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • In an acute-angled triangle, the area of the shape on the longest side is smaller than the sum of the areas of similar shapes on the other two sides.

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • In an obtuse-angled triangle, the area of the shape on the longest side is larger than the sum of the areas of similar shapes on the other two sides.

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • Squares are the easiest similar shapes to construct on the sides of a triangle.

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: These five discoveries confirm Pythagoras' theorem:

title: Note:
content: We can use Pythagoras' theorem to find out if a triangle is acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled:

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • A triangle is acute-angled if the square on the longest side is smaller than the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • A triangle is right-angled if the square on the longest side is equal to the sum of the squares on the two sides adjacent to the right angle.

subject: mathematics
title: Note:
content: • A triangle is obtuse-angled if the square on the longest side is larger than the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

subject: mathematics
title: Points on a compass
content: In the Starter activity, you probably used words such as north, south, east and west to describe the direction from one place to another. These four words represent the cardinal (main) points N, S, E and W on a magnetic compass.

subject: mathematics
title: Points on a compass
content: There is a big difference between the directions shown by the four cardinal points on a compass and so four points halfway between the cardinal points are used: northeast (NE), northwest (NW), southeast (SE) and southwest (SW). These four points and the four cardinal points make it possible to describe the direction of one place or object from another in different ways.

subject: mathematics
title: Examples
content:
• · Description by referring to direction: • » Our classroom faces east.
• » My bedroom has a north-facing window.
• » The clinic is about 6 km southwest of our house.

subject: mathematics
title: Examples
content:
• · Description by referring to places in general: • » Our teacher comes from the northern part of the country.
• » The tourist capital is in the southern part of the country.
• » Most of our mining industries are in the northwestern part of the country.

subject: mathematics
title: Examples
content:
• · Description by referring to particular places: • » Zambia is in southern central Africa and Japan in southeastern Asia.
• » Spain lies in the southwestern part of Europe.
• » The 2014 FIFA World Cup was held in the easterly part of South America.

subject: mathematics
title: Examples
content:
• Description by referring to movement: • » A learner walked 10 km to school in an easterly direction from home.
• » The cyclist cycled southwards and the bus travelled westwards.
• » The aeroplane flies in a northeasterly direction.

subject: mathematics
title: Salaries and wages
content: In our modern society, people need money so they can care for themselves and their families. People can earn money by selling knowledge, skills and time. They earn either a salary or a wage:

subject: mathematics
title: Salaries and wages
content: • A wage is paid based on an hourly rate, multiplied by the number of hours worked or on a set rate for a piece of work, multiplied by the number of piece works completed.

subject: mathematics
title: New words
content: salary: fixed payment for work done over a fixed time period wage: payment based on an hourly rate

title: Computing deductions from salaries
content: Certain deductions are made from salaries and wages. These deductions include income tax and pension deductions. Deductions to trade unions are also made from the salaries and wages of employees who are not in management.

content: The following must be deducted from salaries and wages:

subject: mathematics
title: Computing deductions from salaries

subject: mathematics
title: Computing deductions from salaries

title: Investments
content:
People invest money so that its value can increase. There are different ways to invest money, such as depositing money in a savings account at a bank and buying bonds or shares (stocks). An investment can appreciate (grow or increase) over time.

This means that it grows and its value increases.
In the same way, its value can also depreciate.

subject: mathematics

subject: mathematics
title: Investments

title: New word
content: An investment bond is like a loan, where the person who makes the bond available is the lender. This person or company invests (loans) their money (the principal amount) to the borrower in the form of bonds. They make a promise to pay the person or company back in full with regular payments of interest. Bonds are usually available in set units such as K100. People can buy bonds in units such as 10 units of K100. This means an investment of K1 000.

subject: mathematics
title: Introduction
content: A matrix is an arrangement of numbers (data) in rows and columns in two dimensions in square brackets. The numbers in the matrix are called elements, We can represent any data that can be organised in columns and rows as a matrix. We can represent real-world data such as the habits or traits of a group of people and sport results as matrices. Matrices are used in computer programming, in the medical field and in many other fields. Matrices can also be used to solve equations simultaneously. (Remember, the plural of matrix is matrices.)

content: There are many uses (applications) of matrices in mathematics, physics and computer graphics. One application is in cryptography, which is a system that is used to keep communications secure and private.

subject: mathematics
title: Matrices in cryptography
content: The process of securing information consists of encryption and decryption. Encryption uses a secret key to change information so that it cannot be read. The secret key is a matrix (the encoding matrix). The people for whom the message is intended must use a decoding matrix to decrypt the message before they can read it. The decoding matrix is the inverse of the encoding matrix. Multiplying the encoding matrix by the decoding matrix gives the unit matrix.

title: Polygons
content: We need to define a concept before we can use it. Therefore, let's look at what we mean when we talk about polygons. Polygons can be either regular or irregular. So, we will define polygons and find ways to recognise regular and irregular polygons.

subject: mathematics
title: What are polygons?
content: A polygon is a closed shape with boundaries that are straight lines. This means that if you trace along the edge of the shape, you will end where you started. You can also think of a closed shape as a flat shape that you can cut out of a piece of card or paper.

subject: mathematics
title: What are polygons?
content: We place shapes in different groups:

subject: mathematics
title: What are polygons?
content: • shapes with curved and straight sides.

subject: mathematics
title: Did you know?
content: The word polygon comes from the Greek words: poly (many) and gon (angle).

subject: mathematics
title: Did you know?
content: • · A triangle has three straight sides (tri- means three).

subject: mathematics
title: Did you know?
content: • A hexagon has six straight sides (hexa- means six).

subject: mathematics
title: Regular polygons
content: In this sub-topic you will learn about the properties of regular polygons.

subject: mathematics
title: The properties of regular polygons
content: A regular polygon is a polygon in which:

subject: mathematics
title: The properties of regular polygons
content: • all the angles are the same size (they are equal)

subject: mathematics
title: The properties of regular polygons
content: • all the sides are the same length.

subject: mathematics
title: The properties of regular polygons
content: There is only one regular polygon in each group of polygons (such as triangles, quadrilaterals and pentagons). The drawings show eight regular polygons.

subject: mathematics
title: The properties of regular polygons
content: A regular triangle is called an equilateral triangle and a regular quadrilateral is called a square.

title: Circumscribed and inscribed circles
content: We call a circle that is constructed around a triangle so that the vertices of the triangle lie on the circumference of the circle a circumscribed circle (or circumcircle) of the triangle. The centre of the circle is the circum-centre of the triangle.

subject: mathematics
title: Answers
content: Probability is the branch of mathematics that makes it possible for us to predict the likelihood that something (an event) will happen (occur). It helps us make decisions about choices in areas such as business, weather forecasts, health, education, gambling (betting) and engineering. People use probability practically in every field. This is why it is important.

subject: mathematics
title: Demonstrate favourable and possible outcomes
content: As you have learnt, you can find experimental probability by conducting an experiment and observing the outcomes. However, when identical experiments are conducted, their outcomes may differ. We can overcome this obvious disadvantage of experimental probability by assigning theoretical probabilities to the events in a sample space. These probabilities are based on the results of an ideal experiment.

subject: mathematics
title: Demonstrate favourable and possible outcomes
content: We can investigate this by finding the theoretical probability of obtaining tails (T) when you toss a coin once.

subject: mathematics
title: Using a theoretical approach
content: There are two equally likely ways a coin can land if you toss it, and there is only one way a coin can land with tails facing up. The probability that you will get tails if you toss a coin is \frac{1}{2}.

There is one favourable outcome for the event: {T}.
The numerator shows the number of favourable outcomes.

There are two possible outcomes for this trial: {H, T}.
The denominator shows the number of possible outcomes.

title: Write simple computer programs
content: A programmer translates a flow chart into computer language that consists of certain fixed commands that can be changed to computer code. Many computer languages are used today. Some of these languages are very complicated. To be able to write computer programs, you would have to learn a few of these languages. Looking at a simple language will help you understand how to write a program.

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: The computer language BASIC, although not modern, is a simple computer language. BASIC has the following characteristics:

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: • Every line is numbered in multiples of 10, starting at 10.

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: • · The last line contains only the command END.

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: • · Capital letters are used throughout.

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: • A remark can be included anywhere. It is indicated by the letters REM.

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: • Multiplication is indicated using the symbol * and division is indicated using the symbol /.

subject: mathematics
title: Write simple computer programs
content: A computer carries out instructions line by line. It starts with the lowest number. It does not execute a REM-statement. You can include a READ-statement, which is an instruction to find data from a list of inputs. You can also instruct a computer to print the results. If there are many input values, you can let the computer print the values in a table.

title: Every day counts
content: We see great athletes at the Olympics and at other races. They make sprinting and jumping look easy. The fact is that they practise every day - they do not stand around and watch other athletes practise. They practise all the important aspects: starting a race, building up to the right speed, maintaining their speed, and not allowing spectators or other athletes to distract them. They practise in spite of bad weather, tiredness and distractions.

subject: mathematics
title: Every day counts
content: To be successful in Mathematics, you have to practise your skills. You cannot just watch your teacher explain something, think that you understand, close your books and walk away. You need to be involved. Ask questions when you do not understand something. Listen to explanations. Apply new information. Use the answers that are given in this Learner's Book to check whether you are on track or whether you need to ask for help. If you choose to do these things, your skills will improve. Every day in class can make a difference if you decide that improving your skills in Mathematics is important.

In a test or an exam, you need to read questions very carefully and make sure you understand what to do before you start answering a question. Reread questions if necessary. If you do not know how to answer a question, move to the next question and return to questions you have skipped if you have time later.
